Now follow the rules or cautions to be observed in the operation of this book

The first rule or caution advises you that the secret of your mind, which you wish to announce to an absent friend who knows the art and has the book of the Polygraphia, you should write as carefully as you can on a sheet, in the Latin language or the German, or in any other you wish that can be represented by Roman letters. Then place the sheet so written before you, so that for each individual letter of the secret you may be able to fit an appropriate word. For, as we have shown, in this practice of writing a whole word is taken. We gave an example a little earlier in the foregoing.

II. The second caution instructs you that, as has been said, you should not take more than one word at the same time from an alphabet in one narrative of the public Latin discourse; otherwise you would both confuse the open sense and entirely draw away from understanding the mystery the friend to whom you had written.

III. Third, one must take the greatest care not to skip any alphabet through negligence, without taking from it one word fitting the secret. Likewise one must provide that, whenever one or more words occur outside the sequence of the alphabet, you take the whole upper line or the lower one, and not both.
58 Cautions of the Operation.

IIII. Fourth, care must be taken that whenever the discourse of the open speech has been brought to a complete sentence, the next should take its beginning from a larger, thickened letter, according to the form of the preceding example, in which, according to the sense of the Latin discourse, we took large letters at the beginning and small ones for the rest, in the common manner. When the secret of your mind is lengthy, so that it exceeds the narrative of the open discourse, if much remains you should begin again from the beginning; if little, let the discourse be recalled from any place at will. For no one even moderately skilled in this technique could fail to know where you have begun again. Nor is there need to fear the consonance of the speech, which will always be varied in the manifest narrative together with the hidden one; and whenever it is begun from the beginning, a new appearance of the discourse will follow. Continuation can also be made from the end of the first book through the second.

V. Fifth, we advise that whenever you wish to write on a difficult matter by this art, prepare for yourself a small booklet in which you write your secret mystery in manifest discourse. Whoever sees or reads this booklet will judge that no secret is hidden, and even if he has a suspicion, he will not be able to find any of the things that you write.

VI. Sixth, it must be noted that if you transpose the order of the words throughout the whole Polygraphia, changing it by metathesis in each alphabet, and have written two volumes according to it, one for yourself and the other for any friend, you will write between yourselves with complete security whatever you wish, nor is there anyone living on earth who can penetrate your secrets. This transposition, however, can be done in infinite ways.

VII. Seventh, we forewarn you that one must write polygraphically in one way to a man ignorant of the Latin language, in another to one skilled in it. For the former all words must be written out whole, without abbreviation, distinct, complete, handsome, and entirely legible, without partition, without division, and without confusion, lest, deceived by error, he either think one word to be two or judge two to be one. The things that are set down must be listened to.

VIII. Eighth, provision must be made that the person to whom you write mystically by this art should have a book in every respect like yours; otherwise you would write in vain and fruitlessly to one who does not understand.

IX. Ninth, if you wish this technique to remain forever secret and hidden, write out the Polygraphia anew, but do not set the letters of the alphabet before it, and no one will easily suspect the principle of the secret. But so that no difficulty may confront the writer and the reader of the mystery, let the letters of the alphabet be written on a sheet in the order corresponding to the words, and let [a movable one?] be fitted to the heads of the same. The letters can also be engraved on a copper plate, so that they may be moved from one order into another.

X. Tenth, it must be known that although we do not use the Pythagorean T in German and Latin words, we have nevertheless admitted it on account of the Greek language, so that we might have the doubled twelvefold number. Likewise we have accepted the doubled w as the twenty-fourth letter, which is altogether necessary for us in the German language.
XI. Eleventh, let him who receives letters written from the Polygraphia know
Cautions of the Operation

to be read, since understanding is needed in reading. And therefore, whenever he receives a sheet or little book written polygraphically, let him go to a secret place, and, with the book of Polygraphy opened, which he must have with him, let him examine each word throughout all the alphabets, and note most diligently with chalk on the table, or with ink on paper, what letter each one represents. And when he has inspected the whole letter in this way, let him compose the letters into words, and he will easily understand what lay hidden in concealment.

XII. Twelfth, kings and princes should note that, if they have many deputies in different places, it is not prudent to write to all of them with one kind of hidden narrative. Therefore, so that they may have for each person his own secret mode of writing, let them change the order of the words as many times as they wish to have separate modes. Thus they themselves will possess the modes of writing of all, and none of their subjects will understand the mode of another. For the variable modes of writing more secretly by this art are infinite.

XIII. Thirteenth, it should be noted that we, in order to stop the mouths of those who speak wickedly, [have shown?] the possible truth of this new invention of ours, placing the words in the alphabets of the first [book?] so that they cohere with one another and produce a fitting Latin prayer in the manner of an exhortation and supplication offered to God. Beneath whose hidden narrative [unclear], and to write in such a way to a friend skilled in the art that, if all the men of the whole world came together in one place, they could never find the secret lying hidden beneath the open discourse, provided it had been rightly arranged.

XIIII. Fourteenth, it should be known that in this very invention of our Polygraphy there still lie hidden certain things far better than those written above: namely, how you will be able, in a few days, not to say hours, to instruct a man ignorant of the Latin language so that he knows how to write, read, speak, and understand Latin, not indeed universally in all things, but in a certain manner whatever he needs in his affairs concerning any subject whatever. Likewise, how you may make known to your friend, far absent and knowing the practice of the art, all the conceptions of your mind without writings, and with the messenger unaware, securely, safely, and most secretly, sometimes even without a messenger, naturally and without any superstition, danger, or fear. But let those things remain buried in their hiding places with the rest. The reason has moved us, since it neither pleases me nor is at all advantageous to cast precious stones to the wind and to accomplish difficult things without the fruit of gratitude. Finally, beneath these things there lie hidden no small mysteries of subtlety concerning medicines, herbs, plants, precious stones, rivers, the members of the human body, brute animals, cosmography, astronomy and the seven liberal arts, and also concerning all those things that are in human use, and concerning the universal world, both of visible and invisible things. And, lest we be more prolix than is right, all things that are in the world, by extension of the likeness of the previously shown art of Polygraphy, serve a mystical lesson.

XV. Fifteenth, note that all these things that we have handed down as discovered in the Polygraphy are certain small introductions in comparison with those that still remain to be discovered and written in this very faculty; concerning them we pass over in silence, lest we seem to boast in vain. For we have given to suitable minds an occasion for discovering greater things than we have either written or perhaps been able to discover. Let him who can add, for the completion of this invention, those things that he knows to be useful; but let him who cannot, by no means rashly judge the things he does not understand.
An explanation of those things which seemed rather obscure in the second book of the Polygraphy

In the second book of the Polygraphy, apart from the order and sequence of the words, nothing new is handed down from the first; and therefore one and the same manner of operating will apply in both, and we carefully admonish that all things which we said must be observed in the first must also be observed in the second. Only in the narrative of the prayer is an evident difference seen to have arisen, since that one is composed concerning our Lord, the Son of God, but this one to the mother, the ever-untouched Virgin
Book II

is raised to the Virgin. In the second book there are three hundred and eight alphabets set before the words in order, though under different subjects. For from the beginning the narrative of the discourse is directed to our Lady herself; afterward the Lord’s Prayer is expanded under twenty-four alphabets; then the Angelic Salutation is added, next the Salve Regina, and lastly a brief prayer concerning Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God. In all the books of the Polygraphia care must be taken that one word not be repeated in any alphabetical order, that is, not be placed twice, and that none be omitted, because it would cause great confusion for the reader. Therefore the utmost care must be taken that the copies be in every respect emended and corrected exactly, lest, when writing, you fall into error. But if, through the negligence of the scribe or the carelessness of the printer, you find some word duplicated under one alphabet, erase the last one and put in its place another suitable one, which has not occurred earlier in the same alphabet. Know also that these two books of our Polygraphia serve sufficiently for the promised operation: by means of them you will not only be able at all times to write and announce to friends whatever you wish, very safely and securely, but also, without any suspicion, to make one who is wholly ignorant of the Latin language, provided he knows how to form letters, a participant in and learned in this art, something which we believe was previously unheard of in such a manner. But since this manner of writing secretly, under a long narrative of open discourse, comprises fewer sentences of the hidden intention, perhaps for that reason it will be usable only in great and difficult matters, especially among those to whom leisure is pleasing and labor displeasing. We shall therefore give, in the four following books, easier ways of writing, although they shrink from the suspicion of most observers. In the Steganographia, however, there are richer methods of writing most secretly and without any suspicion, where not a word represents a letter, but each word represents another whole word suited to the mystery. Let us set down an example of this: if you wish to forewarn a friend about some imminent danger, under such a narrative of words: “Melancius, Tiberius, John, and Peter, servants of the Count of Asoto, have conspired for your death, and on the fourth day after Lawrence’s day, at night, they will surround your house; see what you should do.” The Steganographia veils this secret thus: “I beg you, dearest friend, to send me by the bearer of these presents ten florins as a loan, because they are very necessary to me for the construction of a certain building; I shall faithfully restore them to you.” Who would believe, or suspect, that this secret lay hidden in the discourse written above? Let us set the same thing under another narrative as well: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who willed to become man, to suffer, and to die for us, have mercy on me, an unworthy sinner, now and in the terrible hour of my death.” Behold, you now have one hidden sentence of your heart veiled under the bounds of Steganographia by a double narrative, in discourse brief but faithful, which the whole world will not even be able to suspect, nor, if it should search for a hundred years, to discover in any way, even if all the learned should come together. Finally, the aforementioned Steganographia teaches you to hide this very secret sentence of your heart not only by one or by the two narratives written above, but in almost infinite ways, and, if you wish, to announce it very safely, very secretly, and very securely. All the methods of this sort of invention can also be changed by metathesis in infinite alternations, and all things can be written and announced through them. Why, however, the work of the Steganographia remains buried in silence has been said sufficiently at the beginning of our Polygraphia, and therefore it did not have to be repeated here.
Let it therefore lie hidden, lest it be seen by the ungrateful.
An explanation of the obscure matters contained in the third book of our Polygraphia

In the third book of the Polygraphia we have transmitted a newly devised method of writing secretly, indeed sufficiently safe and secure, but suspect, to all who look on, of a hidden secret. For no one, however learned, [unclear] hidden mystery without peri-
Explanation

will find [unclear] of the tradition, since indeed he cannot understand even open writing. We have arranged the fabricated words so that they contain nothing in themselves, but merely represent the letters of the alphabet placed before them; through them you will be able to write and make known all the secrets of your mind to a friend, however far absent, with the greatest security. But those unskilled in and ignorant of the art, when they see the writing, will think it is some foreign language, and will be wholly ignorant of what it contains. But when you wish to write or report something to an absent person by the method of this book, take care first of all that you properly distinguish each and every word from the others, so that each can be very clearly discerned from another, lest the person to whom you write take one for two, or two for one, because that would produce a great error. Let us set down an example of this matter: Abrin madon badis, cadulur pasu, adin loroff masara damis, boda omo dromidrus vares mastron phosat, galos, prosol fane lemoros, aro soca bilneso, hamol heliet rhamil festa doron hubor rodex. In this narration of an invented discourse there is contained this brief secret sentence of a friend warning a friend about danger: Do not come to court, because the king is angry with you. You see how easy, safe, and secure this method is of writing and reporting whatever you wish to a friend who understands it. In all things, however, you must know that care is to be taken, as was said before, that you take no more than one word from each alphabet, and again that you skip no alphabet.
Of Book IV

Whenever you have brought the narration of the invented discourse to the end of the book, if the secret of your mind has not yet been completed, begin again from the beginning, and do this as often as will be necessary. Nevertheless, each person will be able at his own discretion to change these words of ours, improve them, and add more, provided, however, that you avoid a consonance that breaks out disgracefully into sounds.
Explanation of the Fourth Book of Our Polygraphy

In the fourth book of the Polygraphy we have placed words fabricated by us in alphabetical order by a similar method, but in one point alone we deliberately differ from the preceding book. For in the preceding book the words contain nothing else of any proper meaning in themselves, except that they represent the letters placed before them at the head. But in the fourth book, which we now have in hand, the individual words designate the letters placed before them. They have within what they display without, because the second letter of each word always serves the hidden mystery, as we shall make clear in the following example. Ecorach hanasar dulay semalas, chorion suriel anephor scabaras busarat vimalo tropen tumelech amasar. For understanding this mystery, take only the second letter from each word, and you will find this hidden meaning: Beware this man. For the second letter in Ecorach is C, in hanasar A, in dulay V, in semalas E; join these four letters and they will make this word: Beware. And so let one proceed in the rest as far as the end of the book. If any hidden mystery remains to be written, one must return to the beginning as often as necessary, until the secret has been completed in full. In this very secret method of writing, if someone has been trained by long practice, he does not need the book, but will readily compose on the spot words suitable for his purpose. But one who is less practiced in composing necessarily requires a copy of the book from which to write. A copy of the volume will not be necessary for the reader, since without the book he can easily find the hidden secret everywhere through the second letters. Yet in great, difficult, or dangerous matters, this method of writing would not be trusted as sufficiently safe, because the skill of an experienced man could by chance find out the hidden mystery. But this method of writing can be changed by an intelligent man, so that the signifying letters are placed in the third or fourth position of the word, with the words altered.
A brief explanation of the fifth book of our Polygraphia

In the fifth book of the Polygraphia we have presented various methods of writing secretly by transposition of ordinary letters, arranged in such an order that, under their covering, we shall be able safely to write and communicate everything to an absent friend. Now, to speak in our own manner, the progression of the transposition of letters is almost infinite, since from one alphabet by metathesis countless forms arise. First we described a straight table containing twenty-four alphabets; by understanding it, as many alphabets will be able to be composed as there are stars counted in the firmament of heaven. For as many characters as there are in that table, so many times, by the art, hundreds of thousands of alphabets arise in order. After this we set out a reversed table distributively, which will arise so many times into another as often as we have changed the first letter at the head. In the first straight table the [unclear] letter is B, and in the reversed one Z. As often as you put any other changed letter in their place, so often you will find a table new in every respect, and so on to infinity. Then we expanded the first straight table, placing at the head of each transposed black letter, in minium, the letter which it represents, so that we might furnish the reader with an easier method of writing.
Explanation

This, then, is the method of writing: in the first black alphabet take one letter of the hidden sentence, from the second another, from the third a third, and so on consecutively to the end. When you have reached it, remember to return each time to the first order, until by concealing you have completed the secret mystery of your mind. But so that you may see the order, let us set down an example. Hxpf gfhmczfueib gmbt gx hsr egerbd qopma wvz. fxeqk ak tnr qxyz. The meaning of this mystic speech is: Beware this man, because he is evil, a thief, deceiver, liar, and unjust. You now perceive what a wondrous transposition of the letters of the alphabet this table provides, since there is no one who, without knowledge of it, can penetrate this secret. For this method of writing surpasses every common transposition of letters, since each letter is always changed from one series of the alphabet into another. From the reversed table also, which we have expanded in order by a similar distribution, let us set down such an example by way of introduction. Rdkt, ftz nyb, teuqz, fu zf, fd. drgh, vfd. Its hidden sense is this: Beware this man, because he is evil. And note that under the example of the straight table already set down, we make the hidden series from the beginning through the reversed table, and again the circle, as you see, to the beginning of the straight table. Hence it must be considered that one series of writing can be drawn through both tables, just as we have already done in the demonstration of the first example, or, if you prefer, through one alone, as we have shown sufficiently in the reversed table. Nor will it create difficulty for the reader to whom you send the hidden message; he will easily understand everything if he has had even a little experience in the art. The strongest proof, moreover, which increases knowledge, is practice repeatedly exercised in any art.

After the expansion of the tables, certain orchemata follow, in which there is not only a transposition of all the letters, but also a passage of one ordered over another. For orchema in Greek is called transilitio in Latin. And first we marked the leap of the letters in the expanded form; afterward we reduced it into an orchema. In the operation of this orchema, however, a wondrous leap is made. There are twenty-four alphabets in it. In the first no letter stands between. In the sixth, three. In the fifth, two. In the seventh, six. In the eighth, seven. In the ninth, eight. Finally, in the tenth, ten, and so consequently up to the twenty-fourth alphabet, in which twenty-three letters stand between; afterward a return by likeness is made to the beginning. The method in the orchemata for writing a mystery is similar to that which is observed in the tables of transposition of letters: namely, when one is going to write according to the rule of the orchema, from any black alphabet one is to take only one letter, which, once written, the minium shows at the head. For the understanding of this, let us set down an example.
Explanation of Book V

[unclear]. Its meaning is this: Beware this man, because he is evil. When, in writing, you have come to the end of the orchemata, and the begun secret of your heart has not yet been completed, you should know that you must return to the beginning as often as necessary, until the mystery has been completed in every respect. And know that from one orchema of letters there are composed as many alphabets as the diligent investigator may wish to have. Finally, this method of writing by orchemata, that is, by transpositions and leaps, is the safest of all, because there arises a transposition of letters that is not uniform, but varied in many ways. And it should be noted that the true and perfect knowledge of the tables and orchemata, if you are industrious and studious, [unclear] the understanding of all writings which are written out in any way by transposition of letters; and it is a great secret which few know: to be able to find all meanings concealed in any transposition of letters whatever.
Brief Explanation of the Sixth and Last Book of the Polygraphia

In the sixth and last book of the Polygraphia we have gathered together certain characters of the ancients, which they used in place of letters, so that, if anyone wishes to employ from them an alphabet of his own, he may be able to do so, although a moderately skilled person, if he wishes, can devise finer characters for himself. All the synthemata of this book are sufficiently open and clear; therefore they need no explanation, or only a brief one. Yet those things which stand forth as newly invented by us require a definite declaration, lest perhaps they seem to have been set down without reason.

First of all, we made all the letters of the Latins numerical, after the manner of the Hebrews and Greeks, thinking it shameful for us if we should be found inferior to them in this respect. For what of the fact that we doubled certain letters, so that they might suffice for an infinite number, when the Jews long ago did the very same thing, compelled by necessity? And the Greeks, because of the deficiency of letters, admitted certain marks into the number, since they could not double the letters. But we, because we are pressed by a like deficiency of letters, admitted two marks, namely this one, &, which our scribes put for “and”; nor does it matter whether it is written thus, &, or thus, et, provided that it represents six in number. We added another, 9, which our people write indifferently in abbreviation for con and com, and here, in the order of numbers, it represents six hundred.

But by the same necessity we doubled two letters, namely r, z, s, of which r signifies ninety, while the curved z signifies one hundred, the long s two hundred, and the closed s three hundred. Moreover the doubled w, which we placed in the order of the alphabet on account of the nature of the German language, represents the last letter, and in the series of numbers one thousand. Let us set down a tabular example of this new invention of ours for the reckoning of numbers, so that anyone who wishes to know the method may have a definite instruction before his eyes. For what has always been easy for both the Hebrews and the Greeks will not be impossible for us. The table of numbers follows.

By the demonstration of this example it is easily given to be understood how safe and secure this manner of writing is universally, in every language known to the writer, in every cause or business, however difficult, secret, great, or lengthy. Hence, when you have come to 1000, that is, ten times one hundred thousand, halt your step and do not wander farther, lest the multitude of letters, by marring it, confuse the beauty of the writing. Yet the method of the first alphabet, beginning with one, is the more beautiful for wrapping secrets in writing in proportion as it is shorter and simpler. Next it should be noted that at the end of the sixth book of the Polygraphy we have handed down another method of writing by numerical signs, which they commonly call ciphers; under its covering you may safely write to an absent friend whatever you wish, and no one unskilled in the art will be able either to discover or to suspect that a secret lies hidden, especially if the rules we have given on these matters are observed with diligent caution. This is that the sheet be formed in the manner of an astronomical table, as though it contained something pertaining to the reckoning of the stars, namely in such a way that characters of the signs or of the planets are interposed, so that anyone into whose hands it should perhaps fall by chance, led on by its table-like appearance, may think that no secret lies hidden in it, but may suppose that everything pertains to some computation of astronomy.

We have arranged twelve alphabets according to the number twenty-four, assigning them in place of letters; the first of these, that of Aries, begins from one and ends at twenty-four. We advise, however, in great

With similar ease the very ancient signs of numbering which we have brought back to light can be understood and comprehended; through them knowledge of numbers is extended to infinity. For whenever a small stroke is placed above a smaller number, a thousandfold number is designated. For X̄ means ten thousand; C̄, one hundred thousand; M̄, one thousand thousands; X̄, ten times one thousand thousands; C̄, one hundred times one thousand thousands; M̄, one thousand times one thousand thousands; and so consequently as far and as much as you wish to advance in counting, without limit.

It is the opinion of many that the ancient philosophers and wise men of art and nature, if they had discovered any secrets, concealed them by various methods and figures, lest they should come to the knowledge of wicked men. The more learned among the Jews also affirm that Moses, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his account of the creation of heaven and earth, covered ineffable secrets of mysteries with simple words. Saint Jerome too, the most learned among our own, says that in the Apocalypse there lie hidden almost as many mysteries as words. I pass over the wise men of the Greeks, men of no small repute and glory among their own people, who, applying themselves to the writing of fables, by prudent invention handed down one thing to the unlearned and another to learned men in the course of a single narrative. Although, because of the slowness of my intellect, I cannot perfectly imitate these most zealous lovers of wisdom, yet I judge it a beautiful and glorious thing to admire them, and, with what diligence I can, to read and venerate them. Thus, when I consider that they, by their own study, discovered great things beyond other men, I may, applying a certain violence to myself, impel myself to some imitation of them, even among the very latest.
Apology

Nor, as I think, has my opinion wholly deceived me, since through the continual study of reading I have both learned many things that I had not known before, and opened an entrance for my thoughts to investigate more secret matters. For if I am not of such great learning or industry that I dare profess that I have grasped that method of the ancient sages for concealing mysteries, nevertheless I have devised certain methods, not altogether to be despised, as it seems to me, of writing secretly and concealing [whatever you wish], entirely without any suspicion; and these, at the urgent request of the most serene prince, lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince Elector of the Roman Empire, the wisest Maecenas of philosophers, than whom no one has seemed to me more worthy to have this great secret revealed to him, I have committed to writing and reduced into the present volume, not without immense labor, lest this great secret should come to the ears of common unlearned men or of wicked persons. I beg you, reader, whoever you may be in the future, to remember how many evils could be done in the commonwealth by evil and wanton men through this science, if it came to the knowledge of many: adulteries, fornications, conspiracies, betrayals, homicides, robberies, and countless evils. For just as a good and honorable man can, whenever he wishes, securely and without any suspicion from anyone, for private or common advantage, make known and express the secret of his will to another who knows this art, so any perverse, wanton, malicious person, with every obstacle entirely removed, however shamefully, [unclear] of his pleasure, will be able to communicate his evil desire without any suspicion. Nor could trust among married persons any longer remain safe thereafter, since a woman, though previously ignorant of the Latin language, made most learned through holy and chaste words of any language or idiom, could understand very fully the evil and immodest will of her lover, even while her husband reads and praises the letters, and in the same way could send back to him her own desire, as broadly as she wished and most securely, in quite eloquent speech. Indeed, although this science may seem childish to some, nevertheless, if it were made public, the whole order of the commonwealth would be disturbed, public trust would perish, letters, documents, writings, and finally all the very speech of men would be turned into perpetual suspicion. No one would any longer trust letters, however good, honorable, and holy; no one would put faith in epistles, since, however holy and chaste the words might be, nevertheless deceit, fraud, and evil deception would always be thought to lie beneath them; and men would become fearful in all things, and no less suspicious of mutual conversations than of any letters. Nor can anyone become so learned and experienced in this very science of writing secretly and most hiddenly [unclear] sufficient for all things, which he himself has not yet grasped. For this science is a chaos of infinite magnitude, which no one can comprehend. Because, however learned in this

When the ancient Lacedaemonians wished to disguise and conceal letters sent publicly to commanders, so that, if they were intercepted by enemies, their plans might not be known, they sent letters made in this fashion. There were two rounded, rather oblong rods, of equal thickness and the same length, smoothed and prepared in like fashion. One was given to the commander as he set out for war; the other the magistrates kept at home, with their authority and with the seal. When there was need of more secret letters, around that rod they wound a long strip of leather of moderate thinness, or as much as was sufficient for the matter, in a simple round coil, so that the edges of the leather that was being folded, joined closely on every side, met together. Then they inscribed the letters on that leather across the transverse edges of the joins, in lines proceeding from the top.

When the strip had thus been written over with letters, they unwound it from the rod and sent it to the commander, who was aware of that device. The unwinding of the leather likewise rendered the letters broken and mutilated, and the strokes and points of their parts were scattered into very different places. Therefore, if that leather fell into the hands of enemies, they could conjecture nothing at all from it. But when the man to whom it had been sent received it, taking the matching rod which he had, he wound it around to the end, just as he knew it ought to be done; and so the letters, coming together along the same circumference of the rod, again met, and supplied an intact and uncorrupted letter, easy to read. The Lacedaemonians call this kind of letter a skytale. See also Plutarch in the Life of Lysander.

Marcus Tullius. The meaning is that Cicero devised individual particular characters for individual Latin words; with these, if necessity demanded, he wrote an oration however lengthy with very few signs and very secretly. Our Bede in England. On reckoning and speech by the fingers. This invention is found in Bede, concerning the divisions of times. When you say one, bending the little finger on the left hand, you will set the joint in the middle of the palm. When you say two, you will place there the second from the little finger, bent. When you say three, you will likewise bend down the third. When you say four, you will likewise raise the little finger similarly. When you say six, you will nevertheless lift the third, with only the middle finger, which is called the ring finger, fixed in the middle of the palm. When you say seven, you will place only the little finger, the others being lifted, upon the root of the palm. Next to it, when you say eight, the ring finger. When you say ten, you will set the nail of the index finger in the middle joint of the thumb. When you say twenty, you will put the tip of the thumb between the middle joints of the index and middle fingers. When you say thirty, you will join the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace. When you say forty, you will draw the inner parts of the thumb over the side or back of the index finger, both only being upright. When you say fifty, you will bend the thumb, curved like the Greek letter called [unclear], toward the palm. When you say sixty, you will carefully gird from the front the thumb, bent around as above. When you say seventy, you will fill the index finger, bent around as above, with the thumb inserted, with only its nail standing upright across the middle joint of the index finger. When you say eighty, you will fill the index finger, bent around as above, with the thumb stretched lengthwise, namely with its nail fixed in the middle joint of the index finger. To these the same author immediately adds: From the very computation that I have set out above, a certain manual speech can be practiced, both for exercising the wit and for playing a game; by it, when the letters are expressed one by one, a man may convey to another, who also knows this technique, even if he is stationed far away, the words contained in those letters, to be read and understood; or he may, through these signs, indicate necessary matters more secretly, or mock the unskilled as though by divination. The order of this game or speech is as follows. When you wish to indicate the first letter of the alphabet, hold one with the hand; when the second, two; when the third, three; and so the rest in order. For example, if you desire to warn a friend placed among ambushers to act cautiously, show three, one, twenty, nineteen, five fingers; for the letters of this order signify “to act cautiously.”

Thus far the example of dactylogy according to Bede, which is varied in many other ways. For, as was also said before, let the sign of unity be taken to signify the letter A, and so thereafter in order. Let there be assigned on the left hand: one on the thumb, two on the index finger, three on the middle finger, four on the ring finger, or the third from the thumb, and five on the little finger. Likewise on the right hand there will be understood: two on the thumb, three on the index finger, four on the middle finger, five on the third from the thumb, and six on the little finger. With these things so established, let us observe which numbers arise from the addition, multiplication, or division of which numbers among themselves. For example, twelve arises from the addition of one to eleven, of two to ten, of three to nine, of four to eight, of six to six, of seven to five. In multiplication, however, twelve is produced by the leading of four into three, or of two into six. In division we have twelve if twenty-four is divided by two.

Furthermore, when the fingers are merely raised, it signifies addition; but when we touch one with another, multiplication. But if we bend one and raise the other, it must be division. Therefore, wishing to show the letter M, which occupies the twelfth place, I indicate the number twelve, either by addition, or by multiplication, or by division. First, by raising the two little fingers of both hands together with the thumb of the left hand; for the thumb signifies one, while one of the other fingers designates five, the other six, and this number shows the letter M. By multiplication in this way: let us touch the third finger from the thumb of the left hand with the index finger of the right, since three multiplied by four makes twelve; or let us touch the little finger of the right hand with the index finger of the left, which is the same thing, for twice six gives twelve. It could also be done in another way, namely by the contact of the index finger of the right hand and the middle finger of the left, which show six. These again, by the contact of both thumbs, or of the index finger of the right hand with the thumb of the left, signify multiplication of the prior number by two; but twice six makes twelve.

By division thus: first we shall indicate twenty-four, the division of which number by two yields twelve. The gesture about which I was speaking above represents division by two, namely if two thumbs are shown, one raised and the other bent; likewise the thumb and little finger of the left hand, and the index finger of the right bent. For they signify the partition of six by three, that is, two; and twenty-four divided by these shows twelve.

So much for dactylogy, or the speech of the fingers, which can be handled otherwise in infinite ways, by assigning to fixed places vowels, consonants, semivowels, double letters, mutes, and liquids, according as it has seemed good to each person to handle such things. Although these matters appear ridiculous, nevertheless they have very great use, if by a certain analogy they are transferred to other matters. But there are some things of which the author makes mention partly in the exposition of this passage, partly at the end; but since it pertains to the treatment of steganography, let them be deferred for a little while, until that point has been reached.

“There were also, as Bede bears witness.” The sense is: the ancients not only wrote or spoke by means of words, as we do, but also transferred whatever the world contains, and whatever can be grasped by us, by a certain artifice to the things signified. Diodorus Siculus, book 4: “The letters of the Egyptians,” he says, “are very like various living creatures, and the extremities of human beings, and instruments, especially those of craftsmen. For their words are not expressed by the composition of syllables or by letters, but by the form of images, their signification having been handed down to men’s memory by use.” Indeed they write the hawk, the crocodile, the serpent, the human eye, hands, face, and other things of this sort. The hawk denotes a thing done quickly, since this bird is almost the swiftest of all; this notation is transferred to household affairs that are done swiftly. The crocodile signifies evil. The eye is interpreted as the guardian of justice and the watchman of the whole body. [unclear] designates freedom, but the left hand, with [the fingers?] compressed, tenacity and avarice. In the same way also of the other parts of the body, the right hand with fingers spread [unclear] writing, which, preserved in men’s memory by long use and meditation, they recognized at once, from the trace, what those things expressed. Petrus Crinitus too, in book 7, chapter 2, writes that this kind of method of writing existed among the Egyptians. Concerning the letters of the Egyptians, which are called hieroglyphic, there is mention among ancient authors, and this can still be observed on obelisks, on which those figures and images of diverse living creatures, plants, rivers, and trees are carved, signifying the philosophy of that people, as Strabo and Pliny, most weighty authors, testify. For on the obelisks of the kings [Sedotis?] and [Sennosornius?], which were brought from Egypt into the city, the interpretation of the nature of things was marked out by symbols of this sort and by hieroglyphic signs. For in this way the philosophy of the Egyptians is believed first to have been made manifest. This is handed down by the same Pliny and by others. Among other images, however, they were accustomed to mark scarabs, bees, rivers, oxen, and other things of that kind. Further, by the very image of the bee the symbol of a king was indicated, because in fulfilling the duties of life he ought to have no less the sting of justice than the sweet clemency of honey. In the vulture they indicated the genius and majesty of nature, because among these birds females only are found, etc. They also painted many other signs in place of words; on these see Horus Apollo on hieroglyphic letters. See Pliny, book 36, chapter 11, where, according to the more correct reading, “Sesostridis” is found in place of “Sesotidis,” and “Phaeron” in place of “Nuncoreus.” Moreover Strabo, book 17, Cornelius Tacitus, book 15, Caelius Rhodiginus, Antique Readings, book 29, chapter 26, and Volaterranus, book 33, mention letters of this kind, although he writes that they have as yet been discovered by no one.

“There were those who by accidents.” The meaning is that whatever exists in the whole nature of things, whether perceived by the intellect or by the senses, can be turned to the use of signifying in the same way as words do. Hence it is that one may secretly, without suspicion and without obstruction by any person, signify the will of our mind to another in countless ways: through words; through signs that mark words, as through light, colors, shadows, sounds, odors, tastes; through qualities that affect touch; through shapes, sizes, numbers; through the motion or position of any things whatsoever, such as parts of the body; through gestures of the fingers
Exposition.

[unclear] movements of the eyes, etc. All these things, if they are handled correctly and arranged according to letters, syllables, words, and speeches in a fixed order, with numbers assigned to them, furnish human beings with admirable powers, the more excellent in proportion as one is more skilled and practiced in those disciplines which deal with the principles, causes, and accidents of sensible things. Such is catoptrics, which teaches how to present visible signs of things to the sight in an instant, by means of certain images projected far from us outside mirrors into the air, devised to signify some speech; these are easily understood by one who has knowledge of the signs. But in what manner it can be brought about that all things are transferred to the use of signs is not the subject of this undertaking, but belongs to the Steganographia, the contents of which work the most learned man Johannes Trithemius sets out in a certain letter to Bostius in these words, etc.

I now have in hand a great work which, if it is ever published, which may it not be, the whole world will marvel at; the title of its first book is Steganographia. There will be four books, and each will be divided into at least one hundred chapters. I began this work at the urging of a certain great prince, whom there is no need to name. You ask what this work teaches: things astounding and incredible to all who do not know them, which have never been heard since the beginning of the world. For the first book contains more than one hundred methods of writing secretly whatever you wish, without any suspicion, without transposition of letters, without any fear, so that there is no man in the world who by natural skill could know, or even suspect, what is contained in my letters, except the one who knows the art from me, or from him whom I have taught. The words are plain and familiar, free from every suspicion; but [no one?] will ever be able to perceive my intention without the art, however learned he may be. It is a truly astonishing thing. The second book will contain many more wonderful things. By fire, namely, in this art I can make the conception of my mind known to one who knows my art at any distance whatever, at one hundred miles or more, safely, without words, without writings, without signs, through any messenger whatever. If he is seized on the road, if he is questioned even under the harshest tortures, he cannot confess anything about my message, because absolutely nothing is known to him about it. Whatever may happen, my message will always remain hidden, nor could all the men of the whole world, if they were gathered together, trace it out by natural power. I can also do this without a messenger whenever I wish. I can also make my will known to one who knows the art, even if he is silent in prison, though I am far absent, however closely he is guarded, even if he were sitting three thousand [miles?] under the earth. And all these things, most broadly and universally, whenever and as often as I wish, I can do naturally, without any superstition or aid of any spirits whatsoever. I admit they are wonderful, but hear things still more wonderful. The third book teaches an art by which I can teach an unlearned man who knows only his mother tongue, who has never known a word of the Latin language, in two hours to write, read, and understand Latin quite elegantly and eloquently, as much as he wishes, so that whoever sees his letters will praise the words and understand that they are composed in Latin. The fourth book contains many astonishing experiments, but purely natural ones. Namely, I can make my mind known to one who knows my art while eating or sitting with others, without words, without nods, as extensively as I wish, even while speaking, preaching, playing on the organ, or singing, without hindering any other action whatever, so that while preaching good things to one who knows, with eyes closed, [unclear]. The fourth book will contain many other secrets which are not to be brought out in public. All who hear these things marvel at them; among them are many noble and very learned men, who think that these things are either impossible or wholly supernatural. To them and to you I answer what I have answered many: that many things are possible naturally which, to those who do not know the powers of nature, seem impossible or even supernatural. And behold, I speak before my God, who knows all things, that those marvelous things which I have foretold, however much you may be able to write or believe, nevertheless are all purely natural, without any deception, without superstition, without magical art, without
Exposition.

[unclear], without the invocation or ministry of any spirits whatsoever. I have said this so that, if perhaps at some time a report should reach you that I can do wondrous things, you should not, I say, think me a magician, but a philosopher. For what happened to Albert the Great, that most profound investigator of natural things, namely that because of the marvels he performed by the hidden power of nature he was regarded by the common people as a magician, I am certain can happen similarly to me. If you ask whence I have these things, which no one knows, listen. I did not learn these things from a man nor through a man, but by the revelation of someone I do not know. For when, at a certain time in the present year, I was thinking what new thing I might be able to discover that would be hidden from everyone, I began to consider whether I could devise those wondrous things which I have mentioned. After a long imagining, when I despaired utterly of it as an impossible matter, I retired to sleep that night, laughing to myself at my own foolishness, that I had attempted to seek out such impossibilities. That same night someone stood by me, saying: “They are not vain, O Trithemius, the things which neither you nor another with you will be able to discover.” And I said to him: “If, then, they are possible, tell me, I beg you, how they are done.” And opening his mouth, he taught me each thing in order, showing how the things over which I had thought in vain for many days could easily be done. Behold, before God, I do not lie but speak the truth: I have so far taught these things to no one, although many, promising great things, have often asked me, except one prince to whom I write, whom by a clear proof I made more certain of the possibility of the art. Nor is it fitting that others know these things than princes; otherwise many evils would be done through them: betrayals, fornications, and whatever else evil men might wish. But those who use the art well could do many things through it for the commonwealth. Moreover, I can teach all these things in every language of the whole world that I have heard. I wished to make these things known to you, Bostius, for this reason: that you should not think me idle.

Thus far the words of Trithemius. Finally, there are other immense uses of these books of the Polygraphia, which we shall treat in our books on the method of teaching and learning; for whatever these things may seem to be, they nevertheless have more hidden within than they promise on the surface. On the Steganographia, whose principles lie concealed in these books, God willing, we shall treat separately.
The First Book of the Polygraphia

There are twenty-four characters of the signs of the Latin language, which, set in order before the same number of significant words, serve most abundantly in all respects, according to the desire of each person working in this art, for secrets. But the paraphrases are so artfully ordered that they produce entirely Latin discourse, if only one is taken from any given order. And it should be noted that, by reason of our German language, the twenty-fourth letter, w, is taken at the end of the alphabet, while all the remaining letters perform the service of both languages. We have placed the signifying elements in order with such skill that, whichever you take from each line, once the deduction of the sum has been made, concord will remain. Yet care is needed, so that from any line of syntax you take only one, and the monad does no injury to the binary. One must also provide that, whenever you approach the cabalistic operation, you first count all the individual minutes of the night and join them in due proportion to the degrees of the following day. But if the minutes, according to the secret ordinance, do not suffice to the degrees of the day right to the end, the windy runner must by counsel be brought back to the prudent chief-measurer. Nor is it an obstacle if by chance night falls back upon the head of day, since a prudent practitioner in the art can, by voluntary addition, recede from the front by as much as he sees night exceed the light of day. And this is to be understood of the individual chapters throughout the whole work of the Polygraphia. Yet we call that consideration unity, by which the binary, by a known little sign of return, may be made certain, lest it happen to go astray. From the monad, through what has been established, the binary will stand, and it becomes a monad. Nothing is set down here in vain; nothing is adduced without cause or idly. Therefore

we necessarily warn that everyone who wishes to copy this work of ours, the Polygraphy, either in whole or in part, should diligently take care first of all not to depart in anything from our archetype, nor to skip, neglect, or transpose any word whatever. For indeed, if he has omitted one letter or word in essentials, if he has changed a word contrary to its nature, he has made the whole course of the work useless. Therefore let him either copy it properly, or not copy it.

We rejoice that the end of the first book of our Polygraphy is at hand; made more ready for what remains, we judge that we must attempt what the powers of our talent may be. For newly invented things sometimes trouble the beginner, because he whom all follow has no one going before him. The first beginning of any invention is more difficult; after it has been made firm, it brings greater confidence to the author. Therefore, completing the first book of our invention with God’s favor and help, we have divided the whole into three hundred eighty-four small parts, placing beneath each, in order as is seen, the proper degrees of paraphrases. And these form a sufficiently beautiful Christian harmony, sixteen varied stations, with more than two hundred nine thousand phrases duly joined together in every respect. Nothing is lacking here for students of these inventions of ours, so that they may have the fullest knowledge and capacity in mystical, secret, and hidden matters, even those to be reported more remotely with the greatest safety. Of the Polygraphia ... whatever is outside the line, by the common reckoning of the day, has deserted the day, not the night. For the night, always enclosed within the limits of the minutiae and paraphrases, never goes beyond them. Therefore, whenever you have crossed the straight line of the day and have not fulfilled the purpose of the nocturnal syntax, turn the head back to the tail, and, a tying together having been made, let there be a bond of both with each other. Arrange the shadow so that it does not confuse the sun by similarity of sound. Nor be ashamed if, in the first calculation, the day has not comprehended the shadow; rather, count up the minutiae of the lines until the necessary proportion follows according to your wish. You will also be able to make a leap from the first into the second, knowing that in the first creation of days there was made evening and morning, one day. Therefore, when evening has been completed, bring the day back into the following one, and, when the sign has been given by a point known at once to the binary and the monad, fix the mystery. But so that you may be able to avoid this difficulty, divide the great revolutions of our whole sphere by arithmetical degrees, and where day is repeated in place of night, set the mark of Archimedes upon the flying one, lest an untimely ternary block the return to unity by means of the binary.
Book I

For for this reason we have set minutiae before the several degrees by an artful invention, so that in these we might relieve the operator from the labor of counting the paraphrases. If you are industrious, diligent, and studious in those things which we have handed down as the principles of the new art, believe us, you will find greater things hidden than we have promised. Indeed, since many natural secrets are contained in these matters, know this one, not the least: that by the prudent operation of metathesis you will, even when you wish, make a man most expert in this art ignorant, the seeing blind, and the learned unskilled. If the false opinion of the Hebrews were true, this invention of ours would give to each man of eighteen thousand spheres his own methods for writing and reporting, safely, secretly, and very broadly, whatever hidden things he wished in Latin.

The reckoning-system of mortals tries, by art, to imitate nature, which admits no calculation of the monad. Hence, although the instruction of the preceding book of the Polygraphia, through the extension and metathesis of particulars, is as it were sufficient for the universals of this art in infinite progressions of number, nevertheless a certain consideration has moved us to join a second to the first. The condition of light is different in each; but night preserves inviolate, in both, the order of its course. The reader who is prudent, from small things and things not sufficiently brought to exactness, if he is strong in excellent natural talent, will be able to discover more polished things. Whatever visible thing is set in the whole circle of the universe gives ready support for the service of this new art of ours. Air and fire, water and earth,
Polygraphia, Book II

earth, springs and rivers, trees, fruits, flowers, grasses, words, names, accident, substance, stones, sand, dung, filth, things, terms, honorable things, modest things, wood, metals, hard things, liquid things, existing things and non-existing things, history, fable, beasts, brute animals, human beings, draft animals, each and all things that either speech can express or the soul think, furnish the very broad field of our Polygraphia, and promise that the art, so far as it can stand for mortals, will have to be enlarged to infinity. For just as, from unity through the binary, the ternary generates the perfect number in the quaternary, so the consummation of this invention, standing through the quaternary in the binary as a twice-perfect root, gives us an infinite number beneath the minutiae of the things of the paraphrases of Polygraphia. For although among us all our things are terminable, nevertheless many things often occur which seem infinite to us because of the slowness of our understanding. Who will be able to count the drops of the sea? And who will penetrate the inscrutable heart of man? Just as a finite, circumscribable number can, by progression, be led into infinity, so the instruction of this art is enlarged by varied metathesis into immensity. Whatever is seen anywhere in the whole world is in every respect conformed to our instruction, nor is there anything known to us that is empty of mystery, if the method is understood by a master. But we, persuaded by reason, stand under the service of the binary and briefly explain the smallest part of the whole. Nor is there given an occasion by which we might raise our attempt to weightier matters; if it should be offered to us acceptably, we shall not refuse to make more important things manifest to those who desire them.

The third book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins

What, from the beginning of human creation, confused the unity of language? Was it not the division of bodies and the variety of minds? For as Truth declares in the Gospel: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. For the tongue is the instrument for bringing outward those conceptions which the mind has thought within itself. Yet of this ministry of the mind’s secrets to the senses there are many modes, whose properties vary both by use and by art. Use, introduced at pleasure, is common to many; art, however, to few. Indeed no one will readily estimate how much the very unregulated use of speaking among the Germans alone has varied in six hundred years, who has not rather often reread Otfrid, monk of Weissenburg, in the poems of the German tongue. The sea flows and ebbs; men, once dying, do not return again to the present life. Customs succeed customs, and the vigor of mortal minds always declines with respect to better things.

Who today among the Germans, ancient emulators of the Greeks, possesses the old knowledge of idioms? In the chronicles, the ancient histories of the Franks, Hunibaldus, Doracus, and the other writers who preceded us by a thousand years mixed many things said in old verse, in the prose of the German speech, into their compositions, which today are understood by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own idiom among the eastern Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, Rhinelanders, Mosellans, Cologne people, Saxons, Thuringians, daily undergoes notable variation? Men are changed in time, customs vary, minds are changed, clothes vary; the simplicity of languages is altered, the ancient property of idioms is varied; nothing stable is found in human affairs. For there is a vicissitude of all things; variety succeeds the simplicity of minds. Who will be able to reduce this perpetual flowing away, so to speak, to the concord of unity?

But the fact that we add a third to the preceding books of the Polygraphy has not lacked a special reason. For, since the wills of men are various, rightly there are given manifold modes for honorable operations. In those, day illuminates night; in these, however, day lacks light. There light leads shadow around in light; here, however, the blind illuminates the blind, and, existing and remaining sight without eyes, ministers in darkness what it does not have. Here night darkens day with perpetual gloom, and one walking in darkness without light provides blind guidance. These paraphrasms serve all men throughout the world, and in every language transmit any secret safely, securely, and without danger to the cabalistic binary. Latinity moves barbarians to laughter, and barbarism itself produces suspicion among Latin-speakers. Yet it matters nothing or little, since however great suspicion may have been, it will nevertheless contain every most secret mystery. Let the diligent operator recall to mind the rules and precepts which we have handed down, lest he labor uselessly and in vain for himself and for others. For understanding is needed; without it the usefulness of no art will stand. Thus in a few things we have shown the way to the greatest matters, and, with a finite mode, we have given the way to infinite things. From things given and received, greater things are easily prepared for friends. Reader, remember that the retrograde mark can be fixed in every place until you take up the mark of rest. Farewell. From Peapoli, on the first day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

What, at the beginning of the third book of our work, the Polygraphia, we promised, namely to provide for the sake of the semblance of a [unclear] gloss before the inexperienced, we have fulfilled sufficiently, by a concise labor, as an example. We have entrusted the night, safely serving hidden things, to be guided by the shadows of periphrases; we have inserted numbers in the order of four lines all the way to the end, adapted for the use of those who wish to employ them. The places of minutes, having fixed degrees, are three thousand one hundred and fifty, although, if you wish, infinite moments of hours remain for concealing, in every language of every nation of the world, whatever secret matter may arise. The circle, arising linearly from a point, as far as you wish and as the work requires, you will be able to lead back to the path by which you came. If much of the night remains, lead back the dragon's tail to the original tail-place at the head. But the binary is made altogether certain from the known signs of unity. Let him who rages greatly labor greatly, so that he may have something to eat. Nor is there need of great labor to lead wherever you wish that which proceeds of its own accord. Here, therefore, we set an end to the third book of our Polygraphia, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Gentle reader, farewell.
From Peapoli, on the seventh day of the month of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ our Savior 1508, in the eleventh indiction.

Hence the prudent man, understanding and experienced in the science, will satisfy the operation at every time and place. The binary receives from unity, whence it produces the ternary. Knowledge of this cryptology is easy at first sight, after the moon has been illuminated by the sun with even a single point. Although it can also happen that the knower becomes skilled without the guidance of a teacher. Yet I think this is to be understood only in this book, and in none of the preceding ones. Concerning those that follow, judgment will be given in its proper place. Among all the cabalistic modes of secrets that we have presented, the progression of this fourth book, easier than the rest, can be extended to infinity. Therefore it is enough that I have handed down to those desiring fuller things both the form and the cause of the example. The light of understanding easily penetrates all these things. With the possibility of our new invention demonstrated, which has been shown briefly and no less sufficiently, I do not think that on this occasion I myself should be wearied any longer in the same matter, since the method offers a path to infinity, if anyone should need an example for further matters. Nor do I think it at all necessary to recall to memory the things that have been recited in the preceding books, since a discerning reader, if he is studious, can, with the Lord’s help, discover even the greater things that lie hidden in these. We have handed over to the wise and studious man both the material and the reason; if he wishes to use them prudently, he will surpass our work by his own talent. But whoever desires this [unclear] to be more beautiful in the shade, let him join hand and mind to talent, and let him make a path for himself, more beautifully adorned with paraphrase. Let anyone whom these things delight keep fixed in memory that he must always remain within the prescribed circle; if he passes beyond it in any way, the whole operation vanishes uselessly. There are many names of men, and finally there are almost infinite terms for things, villages, stones, and words, all of which serve our purposes. From these it is clear that a book and a method can be made, not impossible, if talent is at hand with diligence, which may surpass our inventions without limit. But he who is of such dullness that he cannot understand these childish things of ours, when will he penetrate the more subtle matters that remain? We set an end to the fourth book of the Polygraphy, to which, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, we join the fifth.
The fifth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, begins

Those things which, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have arranged as best we could in the four preceding books for the completion of our Polygraphy, reasonably require that in the fifth book we briefly discuss the remaining precepts of this instruction, the methods that still remain. Therefore in it we shall give a sufficiently compendious method by metathesis, that is, the transposition of letters, by which a friend may securely, safely, and most secretly write to a friend whatever he wishes. We read that Caesar Augustus used that method of writing in secret matters. Although this method of sending messages is in many ways secure, nevertheless to observers it is always regarded with suspicion, because as soon as the transposition of letters is seen, anyone who is curious at once suspects that something lies hidden beneath. Now the methods of this invention are almost infinite; from these, for a necessary introduction, we have marked out the following for the reader, reserving the rest to be investigated by his talent. First, therefore, we have placed at the head a canonical table of this practice, beneath which we have set another, reversed. In these two tables the root and foundation of the aforementioned transposition is entirely placed, upon which the structure of the whole building is set. For when these two tables have been properly known and understood, no transposition of letters will be able to escape one who works diligently. To these we have joined twenty-four alphabets in order, so that we might give the reader abundant means of transposing letters. The use of these consists, according to one’s wish, in each individually, or, if you prefer, also in all together. If you have secret correspondence with many people, distribute the individual alphabets to your individual acquaintances, but commit to memory what you have handed to each one. To the first, indeed, let the first alphabet be entrusted, to the second the second, to the third the third, and so let it be done in sequence with the rest. But if, because of a multitude of business or of household members, the alphabets which we have marked should not suffice for everything, or if some of them seem too open and evident, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions, the number of which may always remain perpetually hidden. Let us set down an example of this matter: let b be a, let f be b, let p be c, let t be d, let z be f, let c be g, let m be h; so consequently through the whole usual alphabet let it be arranged that between any letter assumed and its substitute three idle and transposed letters lie between. Afterwards four, then five, more or fewer, in such a way, however, that the whole alphabet, as if revolved into a circle, meets together, but each letter is placed for another in its own order in the same series. In whatever way you write it, you must know that it is to be firmly entrusted to memory, lest through forgetfulness

For the transposition of letters is possible in as many ways as—according to the estimation of the human intellect, which, enclosed in a mortal body by temporal operation, does not properly grasp the infinite—a mortal but innumerable number rises up. Johannes Trithemius [Peapolitanus?] to the reader.

Since all the letters of the Greeks and Hebrews are numerical, I have often wondered that the painstaking Latinity of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve for the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews established twenty-eight signs of certain duplicated letters, sufficient for every number. The Greeks, however, with like foresight remedied this deficiency of letters by the addition of four characters. We, therefore, having twenty-four letters, why do we not make ours numerical too, since we can likewise find four duplicated ones? Let us give four as an example, and that will be sufficient for every number: m and final iij; likewise r and final 2; likewise long s and final, or closed, s; likewise closed v and open u. When we add these to the twenty-four letters in common use, we have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers.

And it will be no very laborious matter to grasp this method of numbering for those who already know the letters, if they once commit it to memory. For this invention of ours will be able to comprise many thousands upon thousands in number, all of which can be distinguished and understood at first sight, more clearly than light, without any calculation. Many, less experienced in the art of reckoning, think that this cannot be done so easily by the figures of the algorism, especially in large numbers. For as soon as you have inspected with your eye a number, however great, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. Since this is so easy, it is fitting that we set down the letters themselves reduced to number.
I wrote this on 16 March, in the year 1508.

Behold, reader, you have the method by which every number capable of being written can sufficiently be marked and written with a few letters; their extension, as you see, proceeds to infinity. But, as it was once customary to say in a proverb, “the weary ox plants his foot firmly”: whoever wishes to be content with former things should follow the ancient method of numbering. Here begins the sixth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James the Greater the Apostle at Würzburg

Before every invention and use of letters, in the beginning of the world, when human beings were still rude in intellect and uncultivated in morals, under the rule, shared by alternation, of three intelligences, as certain persons think, succeeding one another in order through one thousand sixty-three years, the influences of the planets in the sphere are said to have presided in their own way over bodies on earth by their influence, chiefly under the governance of their intelligence, whom they called Orisiel, that is, the life-giver of God, for three hundred fifty-four lunar years, likewise four months, and as many days and hours. These things we recount as poetic, not as affirming them.

After Saturn, Venus is set down as having assumed dominion; after Venus, Jupiter. But after Jupiter, Mercury, the fourth ruler in order, adorned human talents with various arts. Under the three intelligences already mentioned, namely while Saturn, Venus, and Jupiter were ruling, they assert that human beings did not have the use or knowledge of letters. Hence, whenever one person wished to announce something secret to another, he did it not by writings, since the function of letters was lacking, but symbolically, by certain likenesses of animals, trees, plants, or of some other sensible things, just as they had agreed among themselves.

The time of Saturn, as they say, gave to human beings morals properly suited to his influence. For it made them farmers, hunters, founders of cities, rude, woodland-dwelling, gloomy, simple, uncultivated in life and morals, living for a long time in the flesh. After Orisiel of Saturn, as those who hold this opinion say, the intelligence Anael, mover of Venus, receiving the government of the world by influence, continued it for three hundred fifty-four years, and for four months, days, and hours; under him human beings began to be more cultivated, to build houses and cities more frequently, and also to discover various manual arts, namely weaving, wool-working, and many other things similar to these. They also began to flow away much more into pleasures of the flesh, and to take beautiful wives, and, many children having been begotten by them from these wives, they notably fell away from natural simplicity. They invented games and songs, began to play the cithara, and more eagerly devised whatever they affirm to pertain to the influence of Venus, following the motion of the flesh.

They named the third intelligence of Jupiter Zachariel; when it received dominion of the world after Anael, it made human beings restless with desire for ruling, to carry on hunts, to make tents, and to adorn themselves with various garments. While he was ruling, in accordance with the quality of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, a great division arose between the good and the bad: the former calling upon God, but the latter given over to the flesh and to the world. Under his rule Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once.

But the fourth mover or angel of Mercury, Raphael, influencing worldly things after Zachariel, began in the one thousand fifty-fifth year of the world at the end of the month of February, and lasted until the one thousand four hundred tenth year of the world; under him the use of letters is said first to have been invented. But the letters then, as they report, were very different from those which the world has today, devised in the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet with time afterward these were changed in many ways, and took on an easier manner of formation and a more cultivated ornament. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the presiding deity of all literature, promising that great secrets of things lay hidden beneath fables. After this, when the human race had multiplied and had been spread everywhere over all the earth, the unity of letters did not remain long; rather, the separation of bodies and minds far from one another discovered different and various modes of writing, about which our narration is long. Plato the Philosopher

[unclear] in the Phaedrus relates that letters and the use of writing, together with the system of weights and the game of dice, were first invented by a certain philosopher named Theuth, and that he taught Thamus, king of the Egyptians. But concerning the other ancient men who are said to have handed down special letters to almost every nation and people, letters that remain in use among them down to the present day, it is not my purpose to set down or describe the account. For all the more learned men among us know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: α, ε, γ, δ, ζ, ω, λ, μ, ν, ι, θ, ξ, π, σ, τ, ψ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is reported to have added four: ξ, θ, φ, χ. The opinion of many holds that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and they also steadfastly affirm that they used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. For they say that great consonance exists between the Greek language and our own, although the long interval of time has utterly extinguished that agreement. That most learned former teacher of mine, Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, the most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, had collected several thousand Greek words which signify the same thing in both languages, Greek and German. And Caesar testifies in the Commentaries that the ancient Druids in Gaul, the priests of sacred rites, used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. But as the Romans devastated the world, they at last violently imposed, together with their dominion, the use of their letters upon many nations.

Finally, the remnants of the Trojans, who afterward were called Franks, in the four hundred and fortieth year before the incarnation of the Lord, having gone out from the territories of the Scythians, with King Marcomer providing leadership, came into Germany and received settlements at the mouths of the Rhine from their brothers the Saxons. Thereafter, for nine hundred and fifty years they waged an almost continuous war with the Romans and the Gauls, as Hunibald is the authority, and at last subjected almost all Europe to their empire or kingdom. Yet they did not abolish the letters of the Romans once they had accepted them; rather, mingled among the Germans and Gauls, they themselves learned their language, and preserved their letters and form of writing.
